analysis.one_liner: Makes firearm straw purchasing and trafficking stand-alone federal crimes with penalties up to 25 years.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Rep. Bobby Rush with 25 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and its crime subcommittee and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create new federal crimes for buying guns for other people (straw purchasing) and for trafficking guns, with prison terms up to 25 years, mandatory forfeiture of profits, and permission for wiretaps in investigations. It also raises the maximum penalty for selling guns to people already barred from owning them. It was named for Hadiya Pendleton, a Chicago teenager shot in a park weeks after performing at President Obama's 2013 inauguration, and for Nyasia Pryear-Yard, a New Jersey teenager killed by an illegally trafficked gun.
analysis.who_benefits: People living in neighborhoods affected by illegal gun violence, who bear the cost of guns funneled to criminals through straw purchases and trafficking pipelines. Prosecutors also gain clearer, tougher tools — stand-alone offenses, longer sentences, forfeiture authority, and wiretap authority — to go after the supply side of illegal guns.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a stand-alone straw purchasing offense: buying a gun on behalf of someone else becomes a crime punishable by up to 15 years, or up to 25 years if the buyer knows the gun will be used in a violent crime [S3].

Creates a stand-alone trafficking offense covering moving two or more guns to someone the seller knows will use them unlawfully, with 15-year sentences and up to 25 years for organizers moving guns with five or more people [S3].

Adds forfeiture of proceeds and doubled-profit fines for convictions, adds the new crimes to federal wiretap and racketeering statutes, and directs the Sentencing Commission to raise guideline penalties, including for people tied to gangs or cartels [S3].

Expands the list of prohibited sellers to include people who intend to pass guns to prohibited buyers or use them in violent or drug crimes, and raises the maximum sentence for selling guns to prohibited persons to 15 years [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Gun traffickers and straw purchasers, who would face substantially longer prison terms and forfeiture of assets. Legitimate gun owners and dealers are carved out: bona fide gifts and legal raffle or contest giveaways are exempted, and licensed dealers are not the target of the new offenses.

drawbacks.text: The bill relies on 'reasonable cause to believe' standards, which its critics could argue sweep in sellers who lacked actual knowledge that a buyer was prohibited or had criminal intent [S3].

Longer mandatory-exposure sentences, including consecutive time stacked on the new straw purchasing offense, run against criminal justice reform arguments about incarceration levels and could be weighed against the bill's deterrence goal [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a targeted law-enforcement measure: it attacks the supply chain that moves legal guns to illegal hands without restricting lawful purchases, and its exemptions protect bona fide gifts and raffles. The main honest trade-off is longer prison terms and broad knowledge standards, which raise the usual concerns about overreach and incarceration but are paired here with serious penalties aimed at organizers and repeat traffickers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its crime subcommittee for the entire two-year Congress without a hearing, a vote, or any floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Rush, a Democrat from Illinois, introduced the bill on February 1, 2017, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S5].
On March 2, 2017, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations, where it remained for the rest of the 115th Congress [S5].
The bill never advanced beyond committee: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote appear in its action history [S5].
All 25 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun traffickers and straw purchasers avoided the new stand-alone federal offenses, longer sentences, and forfeiture provisions, because the bill never received committee or floor action.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun traffickers, who avoided the new penalties

for.name: Rep. Bobby Rush
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill naming it for two teenagers killed with illegally trafficked guns and sought its passage.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Chair, House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or committee vote during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 25 cosponsors were Democrats and the bill never reached a vote, so no roll call exists; its sponsorship was entirely Democratic.

industries.note: The bill would create stand-alone offenses with up to 25-year sentences, asset forfeiture, and wiretap exposure aimed directly at the people who move guns from legal sales to illegal markets. Their gain from the bill dying was the continuation of a lower-risk trafficking environment.

The bill does not regulate dealers or manufacturers directly and exempts bona fide gifts and raffles, but stricter trafficking enforcement raises the stakes for how guns sold through legal channels end up in illegal hands. The bill's failure left the existing enforcement framework in place.
